title: As the hart panteth (Psalm 41 [42])
hookLine: a deer thirsty for water, and a soul asking why art thou sad
carry: why art thou sad, my soul

lines: A DEER ON A DRY HILLSIDE.
cards: Late summer, a dry hillside. A deer comes down out of the trees, sides heaving, tongue out, looking for water. The streambed it remembers is cracked mud.
It keeps walking, head low, because thirst doesn't let you stop looking. Real thirst, after a long run, a fever, a hot day with no bottle, isn't a thought. It's the whole body wanting one thing.
A psalm uses exactly that picture for what it feels like to miss God.

teach.b: Psalm 41 in the Douay, 42 in most Bibles: "As the hart panteth after the fountains of water; so my soul panteth after thee, O God." A hart is a deer.
"My soul hath thirsted after the strong living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?"
The one praying is far from home, far from the Temple, remembering the days of walking with the festival crowd, singing.

teach.h: MY TEARS HAVE BEEN MY BREAD.
teach.b: Now: "My tears have been my bread day and night, whilst it is said to me daily: Where is thy God?" Tears for bread, and people asking, where's your God now?
Then something unusual: the speaker starts talking to their own soul.

teach.h: WHY ART THOU SAD, O MY SOUL?
teach.b: "Why art thou sad, O my soul? and why dost thou trouble me? Hope in God, for I will still give praise to him."
A person arguing gently with their own sadness, not pretending it isn't there, but not letting it run the house either.
That refrain comes back three times, across this psalm and the next, which is why some scholars think the two were once a single song.
In between, a line about being overwhelmed: "Deep calleth on deep, at the noise of thy flood-gates." Wave after wave rolling over. The Church gives this psalm a place at the Easter Vigil.

teach.h: SUNG ON THE WAY TO THE FONT.
teach.b: In the older rite, when there were baptisms, it was sung as the new Christians walked to the font: thirsty deer, going down to the water.

how: Catholics pray Psalm 41 [42] in the Liturgy of the Hours and hear it at the Easter Vigil when baptisms are celebrated; its Latin, Sicut cervus, has been set to music by many composers.

o: an old word for a deer, here thirsty for water
an old spelling of heart, the seat of feeling
a wild goat that lives high in the hills

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.
p: sung on the way to the font

s: a hart is a kind of heart
a hart is a deer, panting after the fountains of water.
the psalmist talks to his own soul
why art thou sad, O my soul? hope in God.
the psalm pretends the sadness isn't there
it names the tears and the taunts, and still says hope in God.

games.q: you're far from home, crying at night, and people keep asking, where is thy God? what does the psalmist do?
o: ask his own soul why it's sad, and tell it to hope in God.
games.why: why art thou sad, O my soul? hope in God, for I will still give praise to him. he argues gently with his own sadness.

practice: Pour a glass of water, or wait for the next time you drink, and before you drink, notice your thirst, even a little. Drink slowly, feel the water go down, and ask what else you're thirsty for right now, underneath.
If you pray, say the psalm's line, my soul hath thirsted after the living God; if you don't, simply notice the thirst and the water meeting.

wordCard.voice: Hart. An old word for deer, thirsty for water, like a soul thirsty for God, talking gently to its own sadness. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: as a deer, the psalm's first word.

carryVoice: Your line: why art thou sad, my soul. Asked kindly, the way a friend would ask. Day one hundred sixty-nine, in the books.
